title: THE KINGDOM IS ALREADY HERE… SO WHY DOES THE WORLD STILL LOOK LIKE HELL?
paragraphs: THE KINGDOM IS ALREADY HERE… SO WHY DOES THE WORLD STILL LOOK LIKE HELL?

Jesus said the Kingdom of God had already come among them. Revelation declares that the kingdoms of this world will become the Kingdom of Christ. So which is it? The answer may completely change how you understand your suffering, your salvation, the return of Jesus, and the battle happening inside your own heart.
There is a question that can quietly shake a Christian's faith.
If Jesus is already King, why does evil still seem to win?
Why are children still buried before their parents? Why do innocent people suffer while corrupt men grow powerful? Why do prayers sometimes seem to rise toward heaven only to disappear into silence?
Why does a woman who has spent years following Jesus still cry herself to sleep?
Why does a man who genuinely loves God still fight temptations he thought he had conquered?
Why do churches still experience division, families still fall apart, and believers still stand beside graves begging God for one more conversation?
And perhaps the most painful question of all...
If the Kingdom of God is already here, why does so much of life still feel like enemy territory?
Don't rush past that question.
Because somewhere between the promises of Jesus and the painful reality of this broken world, many Christians have developed a faith they are almost afraid to examine.
They believe Jesus reigns.
They believe He conquered death.
They believe He is coming again.
But sometimes, when nobody is watching, they wonder why His victory hasn't changed everything yet.
And the answer is not that Jesus failed to establish His Kingdom.
The answer is that the Kingdom has truly arrived in Christ, but its final, visible, universal consummation is still ahead.
That distinction is not theological wordplay.
It is the difference between despair and endurance.
Between expecting heaven to have already erased every tear and understanding why Jesus still calls us to carry a cross.
Between pretending the battle is over and recognizing that the decisive victory has already been won.
And it begins with a conversation that must have startled the religious leaders standing before Jesus.
In Luke 17:20–21, the Pharisees asked Him when the Kingdom of God would come.

They were asking about something Israel had long anticipated: the promised reign of God, the fulfillment of His covenant purposes, the restoration of righteousness, and the triumph of His appointed King.
They knew the Scriptures.
They knew the promises given through the prophets.
Daniel had seen a Kingdom that would never be destroyed (Daniel 2:44). He had also seen one like a son of man receiving everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14).
Isaiah had foretold a child upon whose shoulders the government would rest, whose reign of peace and justice would have no end (Isaiah 9:6–7).
The prophets had spoken of a day when God would judge evil, vindicate His people, and establish righteousness.
So the Pharisees wanted to know when.
When would the Kingdom arrive?
When would the promises become reality?
When would God finally act?
And Jesus gave an answer they were not expecting.
In the Greek text of Luke 17:21, we find these words:
ἰδοὺ γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν.
Idou gar hē basileia tou theou entos hymōn estin.
A close rendering is:
“For behold, the kingdom of God is within you,” or, depending on how the phrase is understood in context, “the kingdom of God is in your midst.”
Those two English renderings deserve careful attention.
The Greek word ἐντός (entos) can express something being within or inside. But the immediate context matters enormously.
Jesus was speaking to Pharisees who were questioning Him, not to a gathering of people whom He had just declared spiritually transformed.
That makes it difficult to argue that Jesus was telling every Pharisee that God's saving reign was already established inside his heart.
Many interpreters therefore understand the phrase as “the Kingdom of God is in your midst” or “among you.”
In other words, the King they were waiting for was standing before them.
The reign of God was breaking into history through the ministry of Jesus Christ.
They were asking when the Kingdom would come while looking directly at the One through whom it had come near.
Imagine the tragedy of that moment.
They were studying the promises while questioning the Promised One.
They were watching for the Kingdom while failing to recognize the King.
They were searching for God's intervention while God's Messiah stood within speaking distance.
And before we condemn them too quickly, perhaps we should ask ourselves something uncomfortable.
How many times have we begged God to reveal Himself while resisting what He has already revealed through Jesus?
We ask for a sign while neglecting His Word.
We ask for direction while avoiding obedience.
We ask for peace while protecting the very sin that keeps wounding our conscience.
We ask God to establish His will in our lives, but we become defensive when His will challenges our desires.
We want the blessings of the Kingdom.
But do we want the authority of the King?
That question reaches deeper than any debate about end-times chronology.
Because the Kingdom of God is not merely a future destination.
It is God's royal reign, revealed and exercised through Jesus Christ, which has entered history and will one day be manifested in its fullness.
The Greek word for kingdom, βασιλεία (basileia), can refer to kingship, royal authority, or the realm in which that authority is exercised.
So when Jesus announced the Kingdom, He was announcing something far greater than a geographical territory.
God's promised rule was being revealed through His Messiah.
And the evidence was already appearing.
The sick were being healed.
Demons were being driven out.
Sinners were being called to repentance.
The poor were hearing good news.
Those whom society considered hopeless were discovering mercy.
Jesus declared in Matthew 12:28:
“But if I cast out devils by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God is come unto you.” (KJV)
Notice the force of His statement.
Not merely that the Kingdom might come someday.
Not merely that people should imagine it.
The Kingdom had come upon them through the Spirit-empowered works of Christ.
The miracles were not entertainment.
They were signs that the promised King had arrived and that the powers of evil were being confronted.
But there is something else we must understand.
Jesus did not come merely to improve human circumstances.
He came to deal with the deeper catastrophe beneath them.
Sin.
Rebellion.
Alienation from God.
Death.
The very things no political revolution, human government, technological advancement, or religious performance can ultimately overcome.
And that is why the Kingdom arrived in a way many people did not expect.
Not first through the destruction of Rome.
Not through a military uprising.
Not through a crown placed upon Jesus by an applauding nation.
But through a King who touched lepers, welcomed repentant sinners, washed His disciples' feet, and willingly walked toward a Roman cross.
Think about that.
The Kingdom of God entered history through the ministry of a King who would be rejected by the world He came to save.
The One who possessed all authority allowed Himself to be arrested.
The One who could command angels submitted to humiliation.
The One who gave life to the dead entered death Himself.
And above His crucified body, the accusation was written:
“THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS.” (Matthew 27:37, KJV)
To the soldiers, it was mockery.
To His enemies, it appeared to be defeat.
To His grieving followers, it looked like the collapse of everything they had hoped for.
But heaven was not witnessing the failure of God's Kingdom.
The cross was central to the King's victory.
There, Jesus bore the judgment deserved by sinners.
There, the spotless Lamb gave Himself for the guilty.
There, the promised Messiah fulfilled the Scriptures.
And when He rose from the dead, He did not emerge as a defeated teacher whose movement somehow survived.
He rose as the victorious Lord.
Colossians 2:15 describes Christ's triumph over hostile spiritual powers through the cross.
Hebrews 2:14 teaches that through death He acted to destroy the power of the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil.
And after His resurrection, Jesus declared:
“All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.” (Matthew 28:18, KJV)
All authority.
Not partial authority.
Not authority waiting to become real only at the end of history.
The risen Christ already possesses universal authority.
And yet...
Wars continue.
Hospitals remain full.
Graves are still dug.
Christians still face persecution.
The devil still opposes God's people.
And creation still groans.
Does that mean the Kingdom has not arrived?
No.
It means we must understand the difference between the inauguration of the Kingdom and its consummation.
The Kingdom is already present through Jesus Christ.
But the final removal of every enemy, the resurrection of the dead, the judgment of evil, and the renewal of creation still await their appointed fulfillment.
The New Testament does not force us to choose between these realities.
It teaches both.
Consider 1 Corinthians 15:25–26:
“For he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.” (KJV)
Read that carefully.
Christ must reign until His enemies are placed under His feet.
Paul is describing a reign that is already operative while the final defeat of every enemy is still being brought to completion.
And the last enemy is death.
That explains something every grieving Christian understands.
You can belong to Jesus and still stand at a graveside.
You can know that Christ has conquered death and still weep when someone you love dies.
You can believe in the resurrection and still feel the terrible emptiness of an unanswered phone call.
Faith does not require you to pretend that death is harmless.
Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus.
The Kingdom's present reality does not erase the pain of living in a world that has not yet been fully restored.
But the coming fullness of the Kingdom means death will not have the final word.
One day, graves will surrender their dead.
One day, the people of God will be raised in glory.
One day, the last enemy will be destroyed.
And those who belong to Christ will discover that their hope was not wishful thinking.
It was anchored in a risen Savior.
This is why Revelation 11:15 is so magnificent.
John hears the seventh angel sound his trumpet, followed by great voices in heaven declaring:
“The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever.” (KJV)
In the Greek text, the declaration begins:
Ἐγένετο ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ κόσμου τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ.
Egeneto hē basileia tou kosmou tou kyriou hēmōn kai tou christou autou.
A close translation is:
“The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ.”
The Greek text uses the singular ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ κόσμου — “the kingdom of the world” — whereas the familiar KJV wording uses “kingdoms.”
The essential proclamation is clear.
The world's dominion is declared to belong to the Lord and His Messiah, whose reign is everlasting.

Revelation presents this announcement within an apocalyptic vision of God's final triumph. Christians differ over the precise chronological relationship between the seventh trumpet and other events in Revelation, but the central promise is unmistakable.
The rule of Christ will not remain hidden, disputed, or resisted forever.
The day is coming when the victory of the King will be openly manifested.
Every rival claim to ultimate authority will be exposed as temporary.
Every empire that imagined itself eternal will be shown to have an expiration date.
Every throne that exalted itself against God will discover that it was never supreme.
And the crucified and risen Jesus Christ will be acknowledged as Lord.
That is not a contradiction of Luke 17.
It is the glorious completion of what began with the arrival of the King.
Luke 17 reveals the Kingdom present in the ministry of Jesus.
Revelation 11 announces the certainty of its universal triumph.
One passage confronts people who cannot recognize God's reign already breaking into their world.
The other assures God's suffering people that the reign of Christ will finally and openly prevail.
The Kingdom has come. The Kingdom is coming. And the King has never surrendered His throne.
This is often called the already and not yet of the Kingdom.
But don't let that theological phrase become something cold and academic.
It speaks directly to the life you are living right now.
It explains why a person can be genuinely saved and still need daily sanctification.
Why a believer can experience the peace of Christ while living through overwhelming circumstances.
Why God can begin healing a broken heart without immediately removing every memory of what happened.
Why Christians can receive the Holy Spirit now while still waiting for the redemption of their bodies.
Romans 8:23 speaks of believers who possess the firstfruits of the Spirit yet still groan as they await the redemption of their bodies.
The Spirit's presence is real.
The future redemption is also real.
Neither truth cancels the other.
Perhaps you know exactly what that tension feels like.
You have forgiven someone, but the memory still hurts.
You have repented of a sin, but temptation still knocks.
You believe God is good, but you are exhausted by a season you never would have chosen.
You know the promises of Scripture, yet some mornings you struggle just to get out of bed.
And in your darkest moments, you wonder whether the unfinished parts of your life mean God has abandoned His work in you.
Listen carefully.
The presence of a battle does not prove the absence of the King.
It does not mean every struggle is automatically evidence of spiritual maturity, either.
Some struggles call for repentance.
Some require reconciliation.
Some call for patient endurance, wise counsel, practical help, or the support of the Christian community.
But the fact that you have not yet experienced the fullness of what Christ promises does not mean His promises are false.
Philippians 1:6 gives believers confidence that the God who began a good work in them will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.
He is not finished.
And perhaps the most dangerous mistake we can make is to demand the final perfection of the coming Kingdom while refusing the present obedience that belongs to its citizens.
Because Jesus did not announce the Kingdom merely to satisfy human curiosity about prophecy.
He announced it with a call to repentance.
Mark 1:15 records His proclamation:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), a command calling for repentance — a genuine turning of mind and life toward God.
It is more than feeling guilty for a moment.
More than being emotionally moved by a sermon.
More than typing a religious response and returning unchanged to the same deliberate rebellion.
Repentance involves turning from sin toward God, trusting His mercy, and submitting to the truth of His Word.
And that is where the Kingdom becomes painfully personal.
Because it is possible to debate the timing of Christ's future reign while resisting His authority over our lives today.
We can argue about prophecy and still refuse to forgive.
We can defend biblical doctrine and still nurture secret dishonesty.
We can speak passionately about the return of Jesus while living as though His commands are optional.
We can insist that Christ is King over the nations while refusing to surrender the private kingdom of our own pride.
And suddenly the question changes.
Not simply, “When will the Kingdom come?”
But...
“If Jesus is King, what part of my life am I still refusing to place under His authority?”
The relationship you know is pulling you away from obedience.
The bitterness you have justified for years.
The secret compromise you keep promising to abandon.
The pride that makes confession feel unbearable.
The addiction you hide behind a carefully maintained public image.
The need to control everything because trusting God feels too frightening.
Perhaps the hardest kingdom to surrender is the one we have built inside ourselves.
And Jesus does not call us to surrender because He enjoys crushing wounded people.
He calls us to repent because sin destroys, and His grace is greater than the ruin we have made.
He did not come to offer a cosmetic improvement to an unchanged life.
He came to save sinners.
To reconcile rebels to God.
To make the spiritually dead alive.
To form a people who belong to Him.
Colossians 1:13–14 says that God has delivered believers from the power of darkness and transferred them into the Kingdom of His beloved Son, in whom they have redemption and forgiveness.
Notice the present reality.
Those who belong to Christ have already been transferred into His Kingdom.
Their citizenship has changed.
Their ultimate allegiance has changed.
Their relationship with God has changed.
Yet they still await the day when every consequence of sin and death will be removed.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
We are not saved because we successfully build the Kingdom through our own moral strength.
We are saved by the grace of God through faith in Jesus Christ, and the King begins transforming the people He has redeemed.
Ephesians 2:8–10 makes that order unmistakable.
Salvation is God's gift, not the reward of our works.
Good works follow as the fruit of His saving grace.
And this matters especially for the person reading these words who feels disqualified by the past.
Perhaps your story contains something you wish you could erase.
A betrayal.
A broken marriage.
A season of unbelief.
A hidden sin that eventually became public.
A terrible decision that cost you something precious.
Perhaps people remember you by the worst chapter of your life.
Perhaps you still remember yourself that way.
But the Gospel declares that the worst thing you have done does not have to become the final word over your life.
Consider the criminal crucified beside Jesus.
He had no opportunity to build a religious reputation.
No years left to demonstrate a remarkable transformation before the watching world.
No impressive achievements to offer.
He acknowledged his guilt, recognized the innocence of Jesus, and turned to Him with a desperate request:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV)
What a moment.
A dying sinner appealing to a dying King.
To human eyes, both men appeared defeated.
But one of them was the Savior of the world.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
The criminal did not purchase mercy.
He did not earn salvation through a lifetime of religious performance.
He turned to Jesus in faith.
And the King extended grace.
That is the scandalous beauty of redemption.
Not that sin is insignificant.
Not that justice no longer matters.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that the Savior willingly bore the judgment of sin so that guilty people could receive forgiveness through Him.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence of our decisions.
But by giving repentant sinners a new standing before God, a new allegiance, a new hope, and a future that their past could never have purchased.
And now we must confront another misunderstanding.
Some Christians hear that the Kingdom is already present and conclude that believers should experience perfect health, wealth, safety, and uninterrupted victory right now.
Others hear that its fullness is still future and conclude that Christians should do little more than wait for heaven.
Both approaches miss something important.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray:
“Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10, KJV)
He taught them this even though the Kingdom had already drawn near in His own ministry.
That prayer makes sense because God's reign was already being revealed, yet its complete manifestation still lay ahead.
We pray for God's will to be done because this fallen world still resists it.
We seek righteousness because evil remains real.
We proclaim the Gospel because people still need reconciliation with God.
We care for the suffering because love is part of our obedience to the King.
We pursue justice without imagining that human institutions can bring about the final perfection promised by Christ.
We serve faithfully without pretending that our efforts can replace His return.
The Church is called to bear witness to the Kingdom, not to manufacture its final consummation.
And that witness is not confined to pulpits.
It happens when a husband chooses faithfulness over betrayal.
When a woman refuses to repay cruelty with cruelty.
When a business owner tells the truth even when dishonesty would be profitable.
When a young believer refuses to surrender to the pressure of a crowd.
When someone who has been forgiven learns to extend forgiveness.
When a struggling Christian finally stops hiding and seeks help.
When a family opens its door to someone who has nowhere else to go.
None of these actions earns entrance into God's Kingdom.
But they can display the transforming power of the King who has already welcomed His people by grace.
And still, we wait.
Not because Jesus is powerless.
Not because His resurrection was incomplete.
But because the story has an appointed conclusion that has not yet unfolded in its fullness.
Hebrews 2:8–9 captures this tension beautifully.
The writer acknowledges that we do not yet see everything subjected to Christ.
“But we see Jesus.”
Those words deserve to remain with you.
We do not yet see every enemy defeated.
But we see Jesus.
We do not yet see death abolished.
But we see Jesus.
We do not yet see creation completely restored.
But we see Jesus.
And because we see Him through the testimony of Scripture — crucified, risen, exalted, and promised to return — we can endure what we cannot yet understand.
This is not an invitation to deny reality.
It is an invitation to interpret reality through the victory and promises of Christ.
The suffering is real.
The grief is real.
The injustice is real.
But none of them is ultimate.
Revelation 21:4 looks toward the day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
Notice what Scripture promises.
Not merely that believers will become better at coping with sorrow.
Not merely that pain will eventually feel less severe.
But that the conditions producing death and mourning will be removed in God's renewed creation.
This is why the Christian hope is greater than simply escaping the earth.
Revelation 21 portrays a new heaven and a new earth, with God dwelling among His people.
The biblical story moves toward resurrection, judgment, renewal, and unhindered communion with God.
The King will not abandon His creation to evil forever.
And the Church does not have to pretend that the world is already perfect in order to proclaim that Jesus is victorious.
That truth should change the way we face tomorrow.
You can work for righteousness without expecting every injustice to disappear in your lifetime.
You can pray for healing while acknowledging that God has not promised every believer immediate physical restoration.
You can mourn deeply without surrendering your hope in the resurrection.
You can resist sin without claiming you have already reached sinless perfection.
You can serve Christ faithfully even when the results seem small.
Because the Kingdom's future is not resting on your ability to control history.
It rests on the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
And one day, the prayer Christians have whispered through centuries of suffering will receive its final answer.
“Thy kingdom come.”
Imagine the day when no child will fear violence.
No parent will receive devastating news.
No grave will interrupt a family's love.
No corrupt ruler will exploit the weak.
No believer will wrestle with temptation.
No heart will be divided between love for God and love for sin.
No funeral procession will move through the streets of the new creation.
And above everything else, God's redeemed people will dwell with Him.
Not because humanity finally perfected itself.
But because the Lamb who was slain is victorious.
The Kingdom will not reach its fullness through the triumph of human pride.
It will reach its fullness through the purposes and power of God in Jesus Christ.
And here is the question I want you to carry long after you close this article.
If the Kingdom's future is certain, what is keeping you from surrendering to its King today?
Not tomorrow.
Not after you fix your reputation.
Not when your circumstances improve.
Not when you have finished enjoying the sin you secretly know is destroying you.
Today.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be misunderstanding every detail of Revelation's timeline.
It would be studying the coming Kingdom while refusing the Savior who offers entrance into it.
Jesus told Nicodemus that a person must be born again to see the Kingdom of God (John 3:3).
Entrance into the Kingdom is not inherited through a Christian family name.
It is not secured through religious attendance.
It is not purchased through donations.
It comes through the saving work of Jesus Christ, received by faith, with the new birth brought about by the Holy Spirit.
And the Gospel calls us to repent and believe.
If you have been running from God, you do not have to keep running.
If you have been pretending to be spiritually healthy while hiding a divided heart, you can come into the light.
If you have fallen, you can turn again to the Savior.
If you have never trusted Christ, you can call upon Him today.
You do not need a perfect speech.
You need the mercy of a perfect Savior.
You can pray in your own words:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me, turn my heart away from sin, and teach me to follow You. I surrender my life to You. Be my Savior and Lord. Help me live faithfully while I wait for Your Kingdom in its fullness. Amen.”
The prayer itself is not a magical formula.
Our confidence rests in Christ, not in the perfection of our words.
And if this message has reached somewhere deep inside you, please don't allow it to become another article you read, feel, and forget.

You do not have to disclose private wounds publicly to prove your faith. But sometimes a simple, honest response opens the door to encouragement from brothers and sisters in Christ who understand what it means to keep walking through the battle.
And perhaps someone you love needs this message even more than you realize.
Someone who has been asking why God has not ended their suffering.
Someone who has begun doubting Christ because the world seems so dark.
Someone who thinks their past has disqualified them from grace.
Someone who believes that if Jesus were truly reigning, their life would not be so difficult.

We want it to be a place where Scripture is opened carefully, questions are treated seriously, wounded people are pointed toward Christ, and believers are encouraged toward repentance, grace, obedience, and spiritual maturity.
Our desire is to make biblical nourishment more accessible to people who genuinely want to grow deeper in Jesus Christ.
But producing, maintaining, and expanding a ministry like this requires real work and real resources.
And this is where I want to speak to you not as an audience member, but as someone who may share the burden of making the Gospel known.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should come from a willing heart, not from compulsion.
And that is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not the suggestion that you must pay to receive God's favor.
But a genuine opportunity to partner in work that you believe is worthwhile.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus Christ is.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Your worth is not measured by what you can contribute financially.
A sincere share may reach someone who has stopped going to church.
A thoughtful comment may encourage a believer who feels alone.
A private message may reach someone who is ashamed to ask for help publicly.
And an invitation to study Scripture may become the beginning of a conversation that points a person toward Jesus Christ.
But we can seek to be faithful with the opportunities God places before us.
And that faithfulness matters.
Because the Kingdom we proclaim is not a marketing campaign.
It is the reign of the living Christ.
We are not inviting people to worship a ministry, a platform, or a personality.
We are inviting them to behold the King.
The King who entered our broken world.
The King who welcomed repentant sinners.
The King who carried a cross.
The King who rose from the grave.
The King who reigns now.
And the King who will return to bring His purposes to their glorious completion.
So when the headlines become unbearable, remember that the kingdoms of this world are not eternal.
When suffering makes you question God's promises, remember that the resurrection has already happened and the final resurrection is still ahead.
When sin tempts you to surrender, remember that the King calls His people to repentance and supplies grace for faithful endurance.
When your past whispers that you are beyond redemption, remember the criminal beside Jesus.
And when your heart grows tired of waiting, remember that Christian hope is not built upon the illusion that everything is already healed.
It is built upon the certainty that Jesus Christ has conquered the grave and will finish what God has promised.
The Kingdom is already here because the King has come.
Its fullness is still future because the King has promised to return.
And between those two glorious realities, we are called to repent, believe, endure, love, serve, and bear witness.
Until faith becomes sight.
Until every enemy is defeated.
Until death itself is no more.
Until the whole creation rejoices in the unveiled glory of its rightful King.
The world may still look like a battlefield, but the empty tomb tells us whose victory will outlast every grave.
